sections.b: Luke tells Jesus' last night, death and resurrection with Mark as his frame but with much of his own: the farewell speech at the Supper (22:24–38), the prayer for Peter, the two swords, the healing of the slave's ear, the hearing before Herod, the women of Jerusalem, three words from the cross (forgiveness, paradise, Psalm 31), the Emmaus road and the meal of fish. The account repeats that Jesus was innocent, shows the people of Jerusalem grieving, and keeps every resurrection appearance near Jerusalem, so that the story can go on in Acts from the same city. It ends where it began, in the temple, with blessing and great joy. Several readings in these chapters, the "Western non-interpolations," are missing from Codex Bezae; most editors now print them.

common: Most scholars think Luke used Mark for the passion and added material from other sources or his own composition.
uncommon: Some scholars (the "Proto-Luke" hypothesis) think Luke had a full passion narrative of his own and added Mark's material to it.

sections.h: Luke's Supper: two cups and "Do this to remember me"
sections.b: Luke's account has a cup before the bread (Luke 22:17–18) and another after the meal (22:20), and only Luke and Paul record the command "Do this to remember me" and the words "new covenant" (Luke 22:19–20; 1 Corinthians 11:24–25). A few Western manuscripts, led by Codex Bezae, lack 22:19b–20, leaving one cup before the bread; nearly all editors now print the longer text, which Papyrus 75 supports. The Greek word for remembrance, anamnēsis, is at the center of the churches' debate over whether the Supper is a sacrifice or a memorial of one. Luke ties the Supper to the risen Lord's meals: at Emmaus he is known "in the breaking of the bread" (Luke 24:35), the phrase Acts uses for the church's gatherings (Acts 2:42).

Luke explains for Gentile readers that the Feast of Unleavened Bread was called Passover (Luke 22:1) and that the lambs were sacrificed that day (22:7). Jesus sends Peter and John to prepare the meal in a guest room, reclines with the apostles, and says how he has longed to eat this Passover with them before he suffers, and that he will not eat it until it is fulfilled in the kingdom of God (22:15–16). The cups and blessings fit what the Mishnah later records of the Passover meal (Mishnah Pesachim 10). Like Mark and Matthew, Luke presents the Last Supper as a Passover meal; John dates the crucifixion to the day the lambs were killed.

sections.h: Sifted like wheat: Peter in Luke 22–24
sections.b: At the Supper Jesus tells Simon that Satan has asked to sift all the disciples like wheat, but that he has prayed for Simon's faith not to fail, and that once he has turned around he must strengthen his brothers (Luke 22:31–32). The prayer has been read by Catholics as a promise to Peter's successors (Pastor Aeternus 4), and by Orthodox and Protestants as a word to Peter alone. That night Peter denies Jesus three times; only Luke says the Lord turned and looked at him (22:61). Peter runs to the tomb (24:12), and the Eleven announce that the Lord "has appeared to Simon" (24:34), the appearance Paul lists first (1 Corinthians 15:5). In Acts Peter strengthens the others (Acts 1:15; 2:14).
sections.refs: Luke 22:31–34; Luke 22:54–62; Luke 24:12; Luke 24:34; 1 Corinthians 15:5; Acts 1:15; Acts 2:14; John 21:15–19

sections.b: Luke says that Satan entered Judas, "who was counted among the Twelve," before he went to the chief priests and the temple commanders and agreed to hand Jesus over for silver (Luke 22:3–6). Only Luke places the warning about the betrayer after the bread and cup, so that Judas has shared the meal (22:21–23). At the arrest Luke does not say Judas kissed Jesus: Jesus speaks first, "Judas, with a kiss you hand over the Son of Man?" (22:48). Luke tells Judas' death in Acts 1:16–20, where Peter says Scripture foretold it.

After the testing in the wilderness the devil left Jesus alone "until his next chance" (Luke 4:13). In Luke 22 that chance comes: Satan enters Judas (22:3), asks to sift the disciples like wheat (22:31), and the arrest belongs to "the authority of darkness" (22:53). Against him Jesus prays for Simon, kneels in prayer himself, and heals the wounded slave. The darkness at noon (23:44–45) shows the hour at its height, but Easter ends it.
sections.refs: Luke 4:13; Luke 22:3; Luke 22:31–32; Luke 22:53; Luke 23:44–45; Colossians 1:13; Acts 26:18

sections.h: The farewell at table in Luke
sections.b: Luke turns the end of the Last Supper into a short farewell speech (Luke 22:21–38), shorter than John's (John 13–17). It has the usual parts of an ancient testament: the leader foretells his death and a betrayal, gives a rule for his followers (the greatest must be like the one who waits on tables, 22:24–27), bequeaths them a kingdom and a place at his table (22:28–30), prays for the one who will lead them (22:31–32), and warns of hard times ahead (22:35–38). Paul's farewell to the Ephesian elders in Acts 20:17–38 follows the same pattern.

sections.h: Two swords and a healed ear (Luke 22:35–51)
sections.b: Only Luke records Jesus telling the disciples to sell a cloak and buy a sword, because Scripture must be fulfilled: "And he was counted with the lawless" (Luke 22:37, from Isaiah 53:12). He answers their two swords with "It is enough" (Luke 22:38). Most interpreters read the saying as a figure for coming hostility, which the disciples took literally; some read it as allowing self-defense; medieval popes read the two swords as spiritual and temporal power (Unam Sanctam, 1302). Hours later, when a disciple strikes the high priest's slave, Jesus says "Leave it at this!" and heals the ear, his last healing before the cross (22:49–51).

Luke shows Jesus praying through his passion. He prays for Simon's faith (Luke 22:32). On the Mount of Olives he kneels, prays "Father, if you are willing, make this cup pass me by. Even so, may your will be done, not mine," and tells the disciples twice to pray not to come into testing (22:40–46). On the cross he prays, "Father, forgive them" (23:34), and dies with the words of Psalm 31:5, "Father, into your hands I place my spirit" (23:46). Stephen prays both of the last prayers, to Jesus, as he dies (Acts 7:59–60).

In Luke the council does not meet at night. Jesus is held at the high priest's house while Peter denies him, and "when day came" the people's council of elders, chief priests and scribes, takes him to their Sanhedrin (Luke 22:66). They ask whether he is the Messiah and then whether he is the Son of God; there are no false witnesses, no charge of blasphemy and no formal sentence (22:67–71). Luke notes that Joseph of Arimathea, a council member, had not agreed with their decision (23:50–51).

In Luke, Pilate declares Jesus innocent three times: "I find nothing to charge this man with" (Luke 23:4), again after examining him and hearing Herod's view (23:14–15), and a third time (23:22). He offers to flog and release him, but gives in to the shouting crowd and the chief priests. Luke's Pilate matches the Roman officials in Acts who find nothing in Paul deserving death (Acts 23:29; 25:25; 26:31). Many scholars think this reflects Luke's concern to show Roman readers that Jesus and his followers were no threat to order, while Philo and Josephus remember Pilate as harsh.
sections.refs: Luke 23:1–25; Acts 3:13; Acts 13:28; Acts 23:29; Acts 25:25; Acts 26:31

sections.b: Only Luke tells that Pilate sent Jesus to Herod Antipas, ruler of Galilee, who was in Jerusalem for Passover (Luke 23:6–12). Herod, who had beheaded John and long wanted to see Jesus (9:7–9), hoped for a sign; Jesus said nothing. Herod and his soldiers mocked him, dressed him in a shining robe and sent him back, and that day Herod and Pilate became friends. Acts reads the scene through Psalm 2, naming "Herod and Pontius Pilate" among those gathered against Jesus (Acts 4:25–27). Some scholars think the scene grew from that psalm; others, such as Harold Hoehner, defend it as historical.

Luke tells the crucifixion with fewer brutal details than Mark and Matthew: no flogging is narrated and no crown of thorns. Simon of Cyrene carries the cross "behind Jesus," like a disciple (Luke 23:26). Jesus is crucified at the place called Skull between two criminals, fulfilling Isaiah 53:12 (Luke 22:37; 23:32–33). He speaks three times: forgiveness for those crucifying him, paradise for the penitent criminal, and trust in the Father with Psalm 31. The sun fails and the curtain is torn before he dies, and a centurion declares him righteous.

On the cross Jesus prays, "Father, forgive them, because they do not know what they are doing" (Luke 23:34), practicing his own teaching to pray for those who abuse you (6:28). The words are missing from Papyrus 75, Vaticanus and other early manuscripts, and scholars debate whether they were added or removed. Stephen prays the same way (Acts 7:60), and Peter tells Jerusalem's people that they acted in ignorance and calls them to repent so that their sins may be wiped away (Acts 3:17–19). Christian martyrs have prayed it for their persecutors ever since.

To the criminal who asks to be remembered, Jesus says, "Amen, I tell you: today you will be with me in paradise" (Luke 23:43). The Greek paradeisos, a Persian word for a walled garden, is the Septuagint's word for Eden (Genesis 2:8). In Jewish writings of the time paradise was the place where the righteous dead await the resurrection (1 Enoch 60:8), and Paul and Revelation use the word for God's presence (2 Corinthians 12:4; Revelation 2:7). Most read the promise as entry into God's presence that same day; Christians who believe the dead sleep until the resurrection place the comma after "today."
sections.refs: Luke 23:42–43; Genesis 2:8; Genesis 3:24; 2 Corinthians 12:2–4; Revelation 2:7; Revelation 22:1–2

sections.b: Jesus' promise to the dying criminal is one of the main texts in the debate over what happens between death and resurrection. Catholic, Orthodox and most Protestant readers take it as a promise of conscious life with Christ at once, with Philippians 1:23 and 2 Corinthians 5:8. Seventh-day Adventists and other Christians who teach that the dead sleep until the resurrection read "I tell you today, you will be with me," since the earliest Greek manuscripts have no commas. The full question, with the churches' views, is on the card at Luke 16:19–31.

sections.h: Luke-Acts and the death of Jesus
sections.b: Luke separates the people of Jerusalem, who favor Jesus and later mourn him (Luke 22:2; 23:27, 35, 48), from the chief priests and rulers who drive the case; yet a crowd with the leaders demands Barabbas and the cross (23:13–23), and Peter later tells Jerusalem's people that they killed him, while saying they acted in ignorance (Acts 2:23; Acts 3:13–17). Jack T. Sanders read Luke-Acts as rejecting the Jewish people; Jacob Jervell read it as a story of a divided Israel, thousands of whom believed. The prayer "Father, forgive them" (23:34), missing in some early manuscripts, may have been cut by second-century scribes who saw Jerusalem's fall as God's verdict on the Jews. Christians used these texts to call Jews "Christ-killers" until churches began formally rejecting the charge, the Catholic Church in 1965 (Nostra Aetate 4).

sections.h: Luke's Easter: tomb, road and room
sections.b: Luke tells the resurrection in three scenes on one day near Jerusalem. Women find the tomb empty and two men tell them to remember Jesus' words (Luke 24:1–12); two disciples on the road to Emmaus recognize the risen Jesus when he breaks bread (24:13–35); and he appears to the Eleven, shows his hands and feet, says that a spirit has no flesh and bones, and eats fish in front of them (24:36–43). Luke stresses a bodily resurrection and the fulfillment of Scripture: the Messiah had to suffer and rise on the third day (24:26, 46). Acts adds forty days of appearances (Acts 1:3).

uncommon: A few scholars argue that Luke's stress on flesh and bones (Luke 24:39) answers early teachers who said Christ only seemed to have a body, and differs from Paul's "spiritual body" (1 Corinthians 15:44).

sections.b: At the end of Luke's Gospel Jesus leads the disciples out toward Bethany, lifts his hands and blesses them, as Aaron blessed the people (Leviticus 9:22), and while blessing them he parts from them and is carried up into heaven; they bow down before him and return to Jerusalem with great joy (Luke 24:50–53). The Gospel began with the priest Zechariah unable to speak (Luke 1:22). The words "and was carried up into heaven" and "they bowed down before him" are missing from Codex Bezae and the first hand of Sinaiticus; nearly all editors print them, with Papyrus 75.
sections.refs: Luke 24:50–53; Leviticus 9:22; Luke 1:21–22; Luke 9:51; Acts 1:2; Acts 1:9–12

sections.b: Westcott and Hort (1881) gave this name to places where Codex Bezae and the Old Latin, usually the fullest text, have a shorter reading: Matthew 27:49 and Luke 22:19b–20; 24:3, 6, 12, 36, 40, 51, 52. They judged the shorter readings original. Papyrus 75, published in 1961 and copied about 175–225, has the longer text in all of them, and the Nestle-Aland and UBS editions have printed the longer text since the 1970s. The SBL edition still follows the shorter at Luke 24:3 and 24:36. The same chapters have two famous disputed passages: the angel and the bloody sweat (Luke 22:43–44) and "Father, forgive them" (Luke 23:34).

sections.h: The Law, the Prophets and the Psalms (Luke 24:44)
sections.b: The risen Jesus says that everything written about him "in the Law of Moses, in the Prophets and in the Psalms" must be fulfilled (Luke 24:44). The phrase matches the three parts of the Hebrew Bible, the Writings beginning with Psalms, and is the New Testament's clearest witness to a three-part Scripture. The Greek prologue to Sirach and a Dead Sea Scroll (4QMMT) also speak of the Law, the Prophets and further books. Protestants cite the verse for a Hebrew canon in Jesus' day; Catholic and Orthodox writers answer that it names parts, not a list of books.

sections.h: The women from Galilee at the cross and tomb
sections.b: Luke names the women who followed Jesus from Galilee and supported him (Luke 8:1–3) as witnesses of his death, burial and empty tomb. They stand at a distance at the cross (23:49), see where and how the body is laid (23:55), prepare spices and keep the Sabbath (23:56), and at dawn find the tomb empty. Luke names them at last: Mary Magdalene, Joanna, Mary the mother of James and others (24:10). The apostles dismiss their report as nonsense (24:11), but the two men at the tomb had given the news to them first.

sections.h: Jesus lifts his hands to bless (Luke 24:50)
sections.b: Luke's Gospel opens with the priest Zechariah coming out of the sanctuary unable to speak the blessing the people were waiting for (Luke 1:21–22), and closes with Jesus lifting his hands and blessing his disciples as he is taken up (Luke 24:50–51). The gesture recalls Aaron, who "lifted his hands toward the people and blessed them" (Leviticus 9:22), and Sirach's picture of the high priest Simon blessing the people (Sirach 50:20–21). Hebrews calls Jesus a great high priest who has passed through the heavens (Hebrews 4:14).
sections.refs: Luke 1:21–22; Luke 24:50–53; Leviticus 9:22; Numbers 6:22–27; Sirach 50:20–21; Hebrews 4:14

sections.b: At the Last Supper Jesus says that this scripture must be completed in him: "And he was counted with the lawless" (Luke 22:37). It is Isaiah 53:12, and the only direct quotation of the servant song by Jesus in the Gospels. Luke shows it fulfilled: Jesus is arrested like a bandit (22:52), crucified with two criminals (23:32–33), silent before Herod as the servant was silent (23:9; Isaiah 53:7), and declared righteous (23:47; Isaiah 53:11). Acts makes the link explicit when Philip explains Isaiah 53 to the Ethiopian official (Acts 8:32–35).

sections.h: "Starting from Moses and from all the prophets"
sections.b: On the road to Emmaus the risen Jesus explains to two disciples "the things about himself in all the Scriptures," starting from Moses and the prophets (Luke 24:27), and later opens the disciples' minds to understand the Law, the Prophets and the Psalms (24:44–45). Luke does not list the passages, but Acts shows the first Christians reading Psalms 2, 16, 110 and 118, Isaiah 53, Deuteronomy 18 and Joel 2 this way. Christian interpretation since has looked for both prophecies and patterns, persons and events in Israel's story that point ahead to Christ.

sections.h: The guest who became host at Emmaus
sections.b: The two travelers urge the stranger to stay with them because evening is coming (Luke 24:29). At table he takes the host's part: he takes the bread, says the blessing, breaks it and hands it to them, and they recognize him (24:30–31). The scene caps a theme that runs through Luke, where Jesus is often a guest who turns the meal into a gift (5:29; 7:36; 19:5–10), and recalls Abraham's guests (Genesis 18) and the saying that some have welcomed angels without knowing it (Hebrews 13:2).

The risen Jesus tells the disciples he is sending his Father's promise upon them, and that they must stay in the city until they are dressed in power from on high (Luke 24:49). Acts names the promise as the Holy Spirit and tells of its coming at Pentecost (Acts 1:4–8; 2:33). The image of being clothed with the Spirit recalls Gideon: "the Spirit of the LORD put Gideon on like clothing" (Judges 6:34), and Isaiah's spirit poured out "from on high" (Isaiah 32:15).
sections.refs: Luke 24:49; Acts 1:4–8; Acts 2:1–4; Acts 2:33; Judges 6:34; Isaiah 32:15; Joel 2:28–29

sections.h: Eating and drinking at the King's table (Luke 22)
sections.b: At his last Passover Jesus says he will not eat it until it is fulfilled in the kingdom of God, nor drink the produce of the vine until the kingdom comes (Luke 22:16–18), and he promises the apostles that they will eat and drink at his table in his kingdom (22:30). The sayings take up the prophets' picture of God's feast for all peoples (Isaiah 25:6) and Jesus' own words about people coming from every direction to recline in the kingdom (Luke 13:29; 14:15). At Emmaus and in Jerusalem the risen Jesus eats with his disciples again (24:30, 43).
sections.refs: Luke 22:15–18; Luke 22:28–30; Luke 13:29; Luke 14:15; Isaiah 25:6–8; Revelation 19:9
